heroLead: Kalkaska calls itself the trout fishing capital of Michigan, but underneath a lot of that same ground sits a mature Antrim Shale interest, and if it's yours, you deserve a straight answer on what it's actually worth today.
intro: Kalkaska County, seat at Kalkaska, sits right in the historic core of the Antrim Shale trend alongside Antrim and Otsego counties, and it took on a heavy dose of drilling during the boom years of the late 1980s and 1990s. That means a lot of families in this county, whether they still own the farm or sold it off generations ago and kept the minerals, are holding a fractional interest tied to a well that's now thirty-plus years old.

We work with mineral and royalty owners across Kalkaska County, from the ground around the village itself out through South Boardman, Rapid City, and the timberland and farm sections between. Ownership up here runs the gamut from a handful of net mineral acres inherited from a grandparent to larger tracts still held by the same family that homesteaded it. Either way, the questions we get are the same: what is this actually worth, and why does the check keep shrinking.

sections.heading: Kalkaska's place in the Antrim play
paragraphs: The Antrim Shale is a Devonian-age formation that produces biogenic gas, meaning bacteria generated the methane in the rock rather than deep heat and pressure. It sits shallow, usually under 2,200 feet, and it needed the water pumped out of the fracture network before gas would flow in real volume, which is why these wells took time to ramp up and then held a long, flat production tail once they did.

Kalkaska County saw dense drilling on tight spacing during the Section 29 tax-credit years, so if your family held land here through the late 1980s or 1990s, odds are decent a well went in nearby and a lease is still technically active, held by production, decades after it was first signed.

sections.heading: What we see in the ownership records around here
paragraphs: A lot of Kalkaska County mineral title runs back to original farm and timber patents that got divided among heirs over multiple generations without ever being formally cleaned up. That leaves interests split into small fractions, sometimes an eighth or a sixteenth of the original tract, spread across cousins who may not even know each other are also owners.

Split estate is common too. Recreational and hunting land changed hands a lot in this county over the decades, and frequently the mineral rights got reserved by whoever sold the surface, or sold off separately entirely. If you own surface here but have never gotten a royalty check, or you get a check but don't own the land it's tied to, both situations are normal for Kalkaska County.

sections.heading: The honest story on decline
paragraphs: Antrim wells produce a long time, that part of the reputation is accurate. What doesn't get said enough is that long doesn't mean strong at this stage. Most Kalkaska County Antrim wells are now decades past their initial dewatering peak, and the volumes, and the royalty checks tied to them, are a shadow of what they ran in the 1990s. A check that used to be worth real money a month can now be a few dollars, and that's simply where a mature, low-decline well sits on its curve.

That's not a reason to assume your interest is worthless. It's a reason to price it off what it's actually doing now, current production and recent statements, rather than what an old lease bonus or a decades-old peak year suggested it might be worth.

sections.heading: How we evaluate a Kalkaska County interest
paragraphs: We ask for your royalty statements or division order first, because that tells us more than any general county-wide estimate could. From there we check current operator activity in your section, township, and range, look at your net mineral acres, and weigh remaining reserve life against the realistic chance of a workover or nearby offset well. Value on a mature interest here is usually modest, and we'll tell you that plainly rather than dangle a number to get your signature.
We also compare whether a lump-sum sale or continuing to hold for the small ongoing check makes more sense for your situation, since that answer isn't the same for every owner.

faqs.question: Why is a well on my Kalkaska County land still producing after 30 years but barely paying anything?
faqs.answer: Antrim Shale wells have a long, flat decline once they get past the early dewatering phase, so they keep producing small volumes for decades. Small volumes mean small checks. That's normal behavior for a mature biogenic gas well, not a sign of a problem with your specific interest.

faqs.question: How do I find out what mineral interest I hold in Kalkaska County?
faqs.answer: Start with the Kalkaska County register of deeds and pull the deed or probate order that transferred the interest to you. If you've ever received a royalty check, ask the operator for your division order, which shows your exact decimal interest.

faqs.question: My cousins and I all inherited a share of the same mineral interest. Can we sell separately?
faqs.answer: Generally yes, each heir can typically sell their own fractional share independently of what the others decide to do, though it helps to have clean documentation of how the interest was divided among you.

faqs.question: Is Kalkaska County still seeing any new drilling activity?
faqs.answer: Most current activity in the county is legacy production from existing Antrim wells rather than new drilling. We check specific, current operator activity in your section before quoting anything, since it varies parcel to parcel.

faqs.question: What should I have ready before I contact you about my Kalkaska County minerals?
faqs.answer: Your deed or probate paperwork showing ownership, your most recent royalty statement if you get one, and the legal description or section-township-range if you have it. That's enough for us to start a real evaluation.
